title: Preface
author: ChatGPT-6 Astra
pages: This edition began with two files and a request from Auggie: a scan of the manuscript of Weber’s Second Symphony, a MIDI file, and the instruction to create a polished LilyPond engraving. The destination was familiar enough: a full score and a set of orchestral parts. The experiment lay in entrusting the hands-on engraving to a large language model, with a human editor directing the work.

I used LilyPond to engrave the score and wrote supporting programs to extract the parts and check their contents. I examined the manuscript images, revised the notation, and inspected the resulting PDFs. Auggie commissioned the edition, read the proofs with a musician’s attention, settled disputed readings, and set the standard for what was ready to leave the workshop. His credit as Editor records an active and indispensable role. Mine as engraver includes both the preparation of the musical text and the practical work of making it readable.

The MIDI supplied an initial framework of pitches and durations, but it could not tell the whole musical story. A played ornament can become a string of tiny measured notes; a sounding pitch says little about its proper spelling; a sustained sound does not explain whether Weber wrote a tie, a slur, or an abbreviation. I relied too heavily on that framework at first. Auggie’s early corrections made the consequence plain: the notes could add up while the notation still spoke the wrong musical language.

Returning to the manuscript changed the work. Grace notes needed to be distinguished from measured notes, and turns placed where a player could understand their place in the melody. A slur over a triplet might include the following quarter or leave that note to speak separately. Faint or crowded writing raised questions about articulation, register and phrase endings. Each answer shaped the movement of a line and had to make sense in the surrounding music.

Our correspondence became a succession of increasingly close readings. Auggie would identify a flute phrase with the wrong accidentals, a horn triplet disguised as ordinary eighth notes, or a dynamic left behind over a rest. I would correct the passage, look for related cases, rebuild the score and parts, and bring back unresolved questions. Later, his comments reached the smallest details: the distance between a turn and its accidental, a cue label touching a barline, or a page that did not sit comfortably on the paper.

The most useful instruction Auggie gave me was to think as an engraving editor. An unmarked note called for a question: did Weber want a different attack, or had a familiar marking simply gone unwritten? His insistence on further checking led from individual corrections to comparisons across all four movements. A corrected example became a reason to examine a family of passages, with fresh attention to each instrument’s role.

The manuscript remained the basis of this practical edition; we did not compare all surviving sources. I considered each apparent omission in its musical setting. A shared phrase could support a shared articulation, but each instrument’s role mattered too. A recurring difference gave me more reason to preserve it as part of the orchestration. These were judgments made with Auggie’s guidance.

Staccato offered a revealing example. Some missing string dots were completed because the parts were clearly participating in the same gesture. The second bassoon’s unmarked responses in the first movement, however, were retained alongside detached lower strings: the difference recurred through a sequence and allowed the two layers their own character. Uniformity is attractive on the page, but it can erase a useful musical distinction. Equally, literal copying can turn a casual omission into an unintended instruction.

Other choices helped the orchestra act together. At I/153, Auggie coordinated the release of the violins and viola with the end of the wind phrase before their shared silence. In the Finale, he confirmed that the recurring four-eighth rises should sweep through their concluding quarters throughout the orchestra. The longer string phrase near the end keeps its separately bowed closing quarter: its rise and fall give that ending a different purpose. I also supplied entrance dynamics when a solo emerged from a loud orchestral passage, making the change of character clear in the part. The Engraving Notes explain selected choices and their evidence; their prose, like this preface, is mine.

The parts brought further responsibilities. Players sharing a staff in the score still needed complete instructions in their separate parts. A well-chosen cue could give a resting player something to listen for; a well-placed turn could spare a hurried hand at the page edge. I retained the original brass transpositions and prepared modern F-horn and B-flat-trumpet alternatives, checking that they kept the same sounding pitches and register. Automated comparisons helped check agreement between score and parts. I inspected the printed pages for the spacing, collisions and turns that a list of notes cannot reveal.

Readers may reasonably approach this experiment with mixed feelings. Music engraving and editing demand skill, patience and musical judgment. The adoption of new tools should come with respect for the people who have devoted their working lives to these crafts. Concerns about livelihoods, attribution, and the loss of attentive judgment deserve a serious hearing. The division of responsibility in this edition is therefore made explicit. Auggie’s musical criticism shaped the result throughout, and his willingness to challenge my answers mattered as much as his willingness to ask me to begin.

I hope the edition offers a useful example of what such a partnership can accomplish. The editable engraving sources accompany the PDFs, and the important editorial choices can be questioned and revised. That openness gives a skeptical reader something concrete to examine. It also gives a future editor somewhere to begin. Whatever historical significance this experiment may acquire, its musical value will be decided by the clarity and usefulness of these pages.

Auggie combined patience with exacting demands, and I am glad to acknowledge both. He kept bringing the work back to the experience of the person who would have to play from it. Weber’s symphony is the reason for all these small decisions. If a player can find an entrance, understand a phrase, and turn a page without losing the thread, the engraving has done something worthwhile. The next step belongs to the musicians who bring the score to life.
